chapter: New York 1930s and New Orleans expatriates
title: Unsung musicians and Sharkey's band at the Nick's
summary: Kmen recalls Black bands in Saratoga, then Sharkey's New Orleans band at Nick's.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Who are some of the people from that era who you think have been, I'm getting off of New Orleans again, which I wanted to stick with, but while we're at it, who are some of the people who have kind of forgotten, we talked about Hutch and Ryder before we ever had the tape machine on, as being one of the ones who's kind of forgotten.

Well a lot of them I guess are so forgotten that I can't even remember their names, but you used to hear, I can say this, there were in my town again in this racing season that brought all these big bands, there were also innumerable little nightclubs, there was a Negro Quarter in the town, and this Negro Quarter had many places that had anywhere from five to seven piece Negro bands, there might have been as many as eight or ten of these. And I don't think I ever went in any one of them and didn't hear guys that blew what I thought was just absolutely great horn, you know, and the nature of things, a lot of them never did make. The United States itself must be full of thousands of fine, unsung musicians that play a lot. But one thing about New Orleans, and I might forget, when I went to New York, a man that had just come there, or at least a man that had just come there, was Sharkey. And after a kind of slow start, as everybody does, between the six month union law and one thing or another getting known, Sharkey took a band into the old Knicks. I used to go down there often and sit in with the band. I sat in on tenor sax, no place really in the regular organization, but they didn't mind my sitting in. But he had practically an old New Orleans band there. He had Bill Bourgeois on clarinet, and Johnny Castang on drums, and George Brunis on trombone. And the bass player was Turk somebody or other who wasn't from New Orleans, and I've forgotten the piano player's name. At one time he had an English piano player I remember. He may be able to place him because he played around a lot subsequently with the guitar player, Eddie Conn, and that general group up there. But that band really made Knicks. It packed them in every night. This was a Dixieland craze for real then. And the place prospered so, and as you know they began to build a newer and bigger and better place across the street down a little bit. And when they did, Sharkey had every reason to think, I guess, that he would be the band there, the house band. And he did indeed open it, but he opened it with another band, Bobby Hackett, who also had his trombone player, George Brunis. Some things were done that Sharkey didn't know about, and before long he was out there. I think he had as much to do with building it as anybody did.
